summary: This document defines an RTCP Extended Report block that reports burst and gap discard metrics, for use in a range of RTP applications.

plainLanguage.summary: When a media receiver throws packets away, the pattern matters as much as the number. Drops that come in one bad moment are a different fault from drops spread evenly through a call. This RFC adds a small report block that counts the packets thrown away during the bad moments, and the packets that were expected during them, so that a sender or network operator can see whether the trouble was concentrated or steady. It is meant to be used with the discard count block of RFC 7002.

questions: what is rtcp xr burst gap discard
what is gmin in rtcp xr
burst discard rate vs gap discard rate
subtitle: An RTCP report block that shows whether discarded packets came in clumps or were spread out.

tldr.problem: The discard count report of RFC 7002 says how many packets the receiver threw away, but not how they were arranged. A hundred drops spread evenly and a hundred drops in one bad moment are different problems, and they call for different fixes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an RTCP Extended Report block, block type 20, that reports how many packets were discarded during bursts and how many packets were expected during those bursts, together with the threshold that separates a burst from a gap. It depends on the discard count block of RFC 7002 and is normally sent beside it.
tldr.outcome: With the two blocks and the measurement information block, a sender or network manager can work out the burst discard rate and the gap discard rate, and so see whether the trouble was concentrated in short bad periods or spread across the call.

today: RFC 7003 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2013, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It registers block type 20 in the RTCP XR block type registry and the burst-gap-discard parameter in the RTCP XR SDP parameters registry, and it depends on the discard count block of RFC 7002.

sections.title: What the Block Adds
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new block type to augment those defined in RFC 3611, for use in a range of RTP applications. The new block type supports the reporting of the proportion of packets discarded by the jitter buffer at the receiver, using the packet discard logic of the jitter buffer algorithms. The discards during discard bursts are reported, together with the number of bursts. The block is intended to be used together with RFC 7002, which provides the total number of packets discarded and on which this block therefore depends, although the metric in RFC 7002 can be used on its own.

The block gives information on transient IP problems. Burst and gap metrics are typically used in cumulative reports, but they can also be used in interval reports. The burstiness of packet discard affects user experience, may influence any sender strategies used to mitigate the problem, and also has diagnostic value. The metric belongs to the class of transport-related end-system metrics defined in RFC 6792.

The definitions of burst, gap, loss and discard are consistent with those in RFC 3611. To accommodate the range of jitter buffer algorithms and packet discard logic that implementors may use, the method used to tell bursts from gaps shall use an equivalent method to the one defined in Section 4.7.2 of RFC 3611. Reporting which jitter buffer algorithm or discard logic was used is out of the scope of the document.

The metrics apply to a range of RTP applications that contain a de-jitter buffer (RFC 5481) at the receiving end to smooth the variation in packet arrival time, and that do not use stream repair means such as Forward Error Correction (RFC 5109) or retransmission (RFC 4588).
sections.plainLanguage:
This block counts the packets the receiver threw away while things were going badly, and says how many packets it expected to receive during those bad periods. The two numbers together describe how bad the bad periods were.

It is meant to be used with the discard count block of RFC 7002, which reports the total number of packets thrown away. The two blocks answer different questions: that one asks how many were dropped, this one asks when.

sections.title: Bursts and Gaps
sections.content:
The terms burst and gap are used in the same manner as in RTCP XR. RTCP XR views an RTP stream as being divided into bursts, which are periods during which the discard rate is high enough to cause noticeable quality degradation, generally over 5 percent, and gaps, which are periods during which discarded packets are infrequent and hence quality is generally acceptable.

The RFC also restates the three fates of a packet. A packet is lost if it fails to arrive within an implementation-specific time window. A packet that arrives within that window but is too early to be played out, too late to be played out, or thrown away before playout because of packet duplication or redundancy is discarded. A packet that arrives within the window but is dropped during decoding by a higher layer decoder, for example because of a decoding error, is not discarded. Every packet is classified as received, which the RFC also calls OK, discarded, or lost.

The discard count metric defined in RFC 7002 reports the packets discarded from the media stream, a single synchronization source within a single RTP session, arriving at the receiver. The term discard here builds on the definition in RFC 3611 but extends it to take packet duplication into account, and reports different types of discard counts.
sections.plainLanguage:
The document divides the stream into two kinds of period. In a burst, the receiver is dropping so many packets that people notice, generally more than one in twenty. In a gap, drops are rare and the call still sounds acceptable.

The threshold between the two is set by the receiver, and it counts the number of good packets that have to go by, before and after a dropped packet, for that packet to count as part of a quiet period rather than a burst.

sections.title: The Block Layout
sections.content:
The metrics in the block report on burst and gap discard in the stream arriving at the RTP system, and the measurements are made at the receiving end. Instances of the block use the synchronization source to refer to the separate auxiliary Measurement Information Block of RFC 6776, which describes the measurement periods in use.

The block relies on the measurement period in that block to indicate the span of the report. Senders MUST send this block in the same compound RTCP packet as the Measurement Information Block. Receivers MUST verify that the measurement period was received in the same compound RTCP packet as this block, and if it was not, this block MUST be discarded.

The block has a fixed layout of four 32-bit words. The first word holds the block type, the interval metric flag and the reserved bits, followed by the block length. The second word holds the SSRC of the source. The third word holds the threshold and the number of packets discarded in bursts. The fourth holds the total number of packets expected during bursts and a final reserved field.
sections.plainLanguage:
The count has to be sent with the block that says which time period it covers, in the same packet. If that block is missing, the receiver is told to throw the count away, because a count without a period cannot be interpreted.

The block itself is four words long: a header word, a word naming the stream, and two words carrying the threshold and the two counts.

sections.title: The Fields and Their Values
sections.content:
The block type is 8 bits and identifies the block with the constant 20. The interval metric flag is 2 bits and says whether the metrics are sampled, interval or cumulative: I=10 for the most recent measurement interval between successive metrics reports, I=11 for the accumulation period characteristic of cumulative measurements, and I=01 for a sampled instantaneous value. The burst and gap discard metrics can only be measured over definite intervals and cannot be sampled, and the value I=00 is reserved for future use. Senders MUST NOT use I=00 or I=01, and a receiver that gets a block with either value MUST discard it.

The reserved field after the flag is 6 bits. Senders MUST set them to zero and receivers ignore them. The block length is 16 bits and gives the length of the report block in 32-bit words minus one. For this block it is 3, and the block MUST be discarded if the length is set to any other value. The SSRC of source is 32 bits, as defined in Section 4.1 of RFC 3611.

The threshold is 8 bits and is equivalent to Gmin in RFC 3611: the number of successive packets that must not be discarded before and after a discarded packet for that packet to be regarded as part of a gap. It is set in accordance with the Gmin calculation of Section 4.7.2 of that document.

Packets discarded in bursts is 24 bits and is the total number of packets discarded during the discard bursts. The measured value is unsigned. If it exceeds 0xFFFFFD, the value 0xFFFFFE MUST be reported to indicate an over-range measurement, and if the measurement is unavailable the value 0xFFFFFF MUST be reported. Total packets expected in bursts is 24 bits and is the total number of packets expected during the discard bursts, that is the sum of received packets and lost packets, with the same over-range and unavailable values. A final reserved field of 8 bits is set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.
sections.plainLanguage:
The header says how the counts were measured and how long the block is, and a receiver that sees the wrong values for either is told to ignore the block. Only two of the three possible measurement styles are allowed, because these counts cannot be taken at a single instant.

The threshold is the number of good packets that have to go by, before and after a dropped packet, for that packet to count as part of a gap rather than a burst. The two counts are then how many packets were dropped during the bursts and how many were expected during them.

sections.title: What the Counts Let You Work Out
sections.content:
The metrics are intended to be used with the information from the Measurement Information Block of RFC 6776 and with the number of packets discarded provided by the Discard Count Metrics Block of RFC 7002.

Together they provide the information needed for statistical parameters. The first is the fraction of packets discarded during bursts, which the RFC names the Burst Discard Rate in RFC 7004, calculated from the packets discarded in bursts and the total packets expected in bursts. The second is the fraction of packets discarded during gaps, which the RFC names the Gap Discard Rate in RFC 7004, which the RFC also calculates from those same two metrics. The details of how these parameters are calculated are given in RFC 7004.
sections.plainLanguage:
The two counts are not the end of the story. Combined with the total discard count from RFC 7002, they let the reader work out two rates: the proportion of packets lost during the bad periods, and the proportion lost during the quiet ones.

A rate that is high during bursts and low during gaps says the trouble is concentrated. A rate that is the same in both says the trouble is steady. The exact arithmetic is set out in RFC 7004.

sections.title: Voice-over-IP Considerations
sections.content:
The metrics block is applicable to a broad range of RTP applications. Where it is used with a Voice-over-IP application and no stream repair means is available, the RFC sets out further considerations.

RTCP XR views a call as being divided into bursts, which are periods during which the discard rate is high enough to cause noticeable call quality degradation, generally over 5 percent, and gaps, during which discarded packets are infrequent and the call quality is generally acceptable.

If voice activity detection is used, the burst and gap duration shall be determined as if silence packets had been sent, so a period of silence in excess of Gmin packets will terminate a burst condition. The recommended value for the threshold Gmin in RFC 3611 results in a burst being a period of time during which the call quality is degraded to a similar extent to a typical pulse code modulation severely errored second.
sections.plainLanguage:
For a voice call, the same two kinds of period apply, with the same threshold of about one dropped packet in twenty.

One adjustment is needed for calls that go quiet when nobody is speaking. The length of a burst or a gap is measured as if the silence packets had been sent, so that a quiet spell ends the burst rather than extending it.

sections.title: Signalling the Block with SDP
sections.content:
RFC 3611 defines the use of SDP (RFC 4566) for signalling the use of XR blocks, although XR blocks MAY be used without prior signalling.

This RFC extends the rtcp-xr SDP attribute of RFC 3611 with an additional value of xr-format to signal the use of the report block defined here. The ABNF is xr-format =/ xr-bgd-block and xr-bgd-block = "burst-gap-discard". Where SDP is used in an offer and answer context, the unilateral rtcp-xr attribute parameter usage defined in Section 5.2 of RFC 3611 applies.

IANA has assigned the block type value 20 in the RTCP XR Block Type Registry to the Burst/Gap Discard Metrics Block, and the new parameter burst-gap-discard in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The block can be used without any negotiation. If the two ends want to agree on it first, it is announced in the session description, in the same attribute used for the other extended report blocks, with the value burst-gap-discard.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: It is believed that this RTCP XR block introduces no new security considerations beyond those described in RFC 3611. The block does not provide per-packet statistics, so the risk to confidentiality documented in Section 7, paragraph 3 of RFC 3611 does not apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The block adds no new security risk, because it reports summary counts rather than anything about individual packets.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Interval metric flag: interval or cumulative only.

fields.name: resv
fields.desc: Reserved bits; senders set them to zero and receivers ignore them.

fields.name: Block Length
fields.desc: Length of the block in 32-bit words minus one.

fields.name: SSRC of Source
fields.desc: The synchronization source the counts belong to.

fields.name: Threshold
fields.desc: The number of successive packets that must not be discarded for a discard to count as part of a gap.

fields.name: Packets Discarded in Bursts
fields.desc: The total number of packets discarded during the discard bursts.

fields.name: Total Packets Expected in Bursts
fields.desc: The total number of packets expected during the discard bursts, received plus lost.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved bits; senders set them to zero and receivers ignore them.

Discarded packets are infrequent and hence quality is generally acceptable

viz.caption: WHAT THE TWO COUNTS AND THE OTHER BLOCKS LET YOU WORK OUT

items.title: Burst discard rate
items.text: The fraction of packets discarded during bursts, calculated from the packets discarded in bursts and the packets expected in bursts.

items.title: Gap discard rate
items.text: The fraction of packets discarded during gaps, calculated by RFC 7004 from the same two metrics.

items.title: Total discarded
items.text: The number of packets discarded in the period, taken from the Discard Count Metrics Block of RFC 7002.

items.title: The period itself
items.text: The span of the report, taken from the Measurement Information Block of RFC 6776, which has to arrive in the same packet.
